title: Adaptation of Computer Use Agentsto New Software with User Manuals

paper.title: Adaptation of Computer Use Agents to New Software with User Manuals
paper.abstract:
Abstract Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have significantly improved the ability to operate real-world software through graphical user interfaces (GUIs) using visual observations and natural language instructions.
However, maintaining strong performance on unseen applications remains challenging, as practical tasks often require long-horizon procedural knowledge and application-specific operation patterns.
In addition, constructing executable tasks and collecting corresponding trajectories for training still heavily rely on human-annotated data, incurring substantial cost.
In this paper, we propose MAGE (Manual-augmented computer use AG ent E xecution and learning), a framework that leverages user manuals as a scalable source of procedural knowledge to improve both inference and training.
During execution, MAGE retrieves task-relevant manual content and uses a planner to generate explicit procedural guidance for CUAs.
To further account for the discrepancies between manuals and actual GUI environments, such as version differences or user settings, MAGE also adapts the agent policy through environment interaction.
During training, MAGE converts manuals into executable task-plan pairs and uses the plans to guide environment rollouts toward task-relevant states; the resulting trajectories are then used to optimize the policy without human-authored demonstrations.
This unified design enables effective utilization of manuals for both task execution and training, reducing reliance on human-authored training data.
Experimental results across six applications demonstrate improvements in task success rates over strong baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of manual-guided planning and policy adaptation in new software environments.
We provide the code and reproduction scripts at https://github.com/ku-autoai/MAGE.git .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent advances in multimodal vision-language models (VLMs) ( Yin et al., 2024 ) have enabled Computer Use Agents (CUAs) ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) to operate software from visual observations and natural language instructions. Unlike conventional automation methods that rely on APIs or HTML structures, these agents interact directly with graphical user interfaces (GUIs) in a human-like manner. This enables CUAs to perform various tasks across diverse software environments. However, existing CUAs require additional training to maintain high performance on unfamiliar applications since each application has its own interface and functionalities. Existing adaptation ( Qin et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) typically relies on costly human annotations to define diverse executable tasks and collect corresponding action trajectories. Although reinforcement learning ( Sutton et al., 1998 ; Silver and Sutton, 2025 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) can reduce the need for human demonstrations, GUI tasks are inherently long-horizon: agents should sequentially uncover available options through clicks, menus, and dialogs rather than observing all relevant information at once. This makes it difficult to obtain sufficient successful trajectories, limiting the training signals required to improve the agent policy. To address these limitations, we leverage user manuals as a source of procedural supervision. Manuals describe application functionalities and the procedures required to execute them, including functions hidden behind menus, dialogs, and toolbars. By exposing access routes to such functions, manuals can reduce unguided exploration in long-horizon GUI tasks. Prior approaches have also leveraged external knowledge, such as web tutorials and past interaction experiences, to guide GUI agents ( Xu et al., 2025a ; Agashe et al., 2025 ) . However, providing external knowledge only during execution does not directly address the challenge of collecting successful trajectories for policy adaptation. Moreover, manuals may be abstract or differ from actual GUI environments due to software versions, user settings, or access permissions. Thus, agents must ground procedural guidance through environment interaction and learn which actions succeed in the current GUI state. Based on this observation, we propose MAGE (Manual-augmented computer use AG ent E xecution and learning), a unified framework that leverages user manuals to improve both execution-time planning and training-time policy optimization. During execution, MAGE retrieves task-relevant manual content and uses a planner to generate task-specific procedural plans that guide CUAs. During training, it automatically generates diverse executable tasks and corresponding plans from user manuals. Rather than treating generated plans as expert demonstrations, MAGE evaluates the collected trajectories and optimizes the agent policy using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). This joint use of manuals for planning and policy learning enables application-specific adaptation without human-authored demonstrations or step-level action annotations. Our main contributions are summarized as follows. • We propose MAGE, a unified framework that uses user manuals as procedural supervision for both execution-time planning and training-time policy learning, combining a planner with CUAs. • We introduce retrieval-augmented planning, which retrieves task-relevant manual content and generates procedural plans to guide long-horizon GUI execution. • We develop a manual-derived training method that constructs task-plan pairs and optimizes the policy from the resulting trajectories without human-authored demonstrations or step-level annotations. • We evaluate MAGE across six applications and demonstrate improvements in task success rates over the corresponding baselines, examining the contributions of manual-guided planning and policy optimization.

sections.heading: Computer use agents (CUAs)
sections.text: To mitigate reliance on specific interfaces or predefined structural representations in computer environments, VLM-based agents that understand GUIs purely from visual signals have been proposed, with representative examples including OpenCUA ( Wang et al., 2025 ) and UI-TARS ( Qin et al., 2025 ) . Training these foundation models requires large and diverse datasets. For instance, OpenCUA ( Wang et al., 2025 ) integrates datasets from prior works such as ShowUI ( Lin et al., 2024 ) and UGround ( Qian et al., 2025 ) , along with general supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data from the Kimi Team ( Team et al., 2025 ) , and further incorporates demonstration data collected from Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS environments. Similarly, UI-TARS ( Qin et al., 2025 ) constructs additional training data by allowing human annotators to refine and correct trajectories generated by the model. While such data-centric training strategies significantly improve model performance, adapting these models to new software environments requires additional data collection and annotation tailored to each target domain. This process incurs substantial cost, thereby limiting the scalability and practical applicability of CUAs.

sections.heading: Reducing human supervision for CUA adaptation
sections.text: Prior work has explored reducing human supervision for CUA adaptation by augmenting or reusing existing datasets for training, or by leveraging external knowledge to guide task execution. BTL-UI ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) augments existing datasets with ROI annotations, while ZeroGUI ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and DART ( Li et al., 2025 ) leverage benchmark-derived tasks for reinforcement learning. Meanwhile, RAG-GUI ( Xu et al., 2025a ) trains a VLM to generate guidelines from web tutorials, guiding a frozen CUA at inference time, and Agent S ( Agashe et al., 2025 ) uses external knowledge for hierarchical planning. However, data-driven approaches still rely on task-specific data, while knowledge-based approaches primarily assist execution at inference time without adapting the CUA’s policy. In contrast, MAGE leverages user manuals for both planning and policy optimization, improving task execution without repeatedly generating plans throughout an episode.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: MAGE is a manual-augmented adaptation framework for CUAs. Given a target program and its user manual, MAGE uses the manual as procedural supervision in two complementary ways: it retrieves task-relevant instructions to guide long-horizon execution, and it generates executable task-plan pairs to support policy training. These two components address the main bottlenecks in GUI adaptation: reliable task execution and scalable collection of successful trajectories.

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem Definition
sections.text: Given a natural language task instruction ℐ \mathcal{I} , our goal is to complete the task ℐ \mathcal{I} by performing a sequence of actions. At each time step t t , the agent observes a screenshot o t o_{t} , generates an action a t a_{t} , and receives the next observation o t + 1 o_{t+1} . This process forms a trajectory τ = { ( o 1 , a 1 ) , ( o 2 , a 2 ) , … , ( o T , a T ) } \tau=\{(o_{1},a_{1}),(o_{2},a_{2}),\dots,(o_{T},a_{T})\} where T T is the length of the trajectory. The action space includes common mouse and keyboard actions such as click, right click, double click, scroll, drag, and typing. Please refer to Appendix E for the detailed descriptions of each action and its arguments.

sections.heading: 3.2 Task Execution with Retrieval-Augmented Planning
sections.text: Figure 1: Task execution with user manuals. MAGE retrieves relevant manual sections, then generates a retrieval-augmented plan, and finally performs GUI task execution conditioned on the plan. CUAs execute a task by repeatedly selecting the most appropriate action a t a_{t} based on the current observation o t o_{t} and the past trajectory τ < t = { ( o j , a j ) | 1 ≤ j < t } \tau_{<t}=\{(o_{j},a_{j})|1\leq j<t\} . However, in many GUI environments, the information required for the task completion is not fully visible in the current screenshot. Important functions are often hidden behind menus, dialogs, toolbars, or keyboard shortcuts, degrading the performance of agents for long-horizon tasks. To address the problem, we propose retrieval-augmented planning which uses procedural guidance from user manuals during task execution. As shown in Figure 1 , our task execution consists of two stages. In the first stage, MAGE performs retrieval-augmented planning, following the retrieval-augmented generation framework ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) . It first retrieves relevant manual sections to provide detailed procedural information to the planner and generates an execution plan consisting of a sequence of actions with specific information such as button names and keyboard shortcuts. In the next stage, MAGE executes the task similarly to conventional CUAs but with the execution plan.

sections.heading: 3.3 Training CUAs with Manual-Derived Tasks
sections.text: Figure 2: Training CUAs with a user manual. MAGE uses manual-derived task-plan pairs to collect episodes for policy optimization. Retrieval-augmented planning provides procedural guidance, but manuals do not fully specify the actual GUI state of a target environment. In addition, interface elements can be hidden, customized, or restricted depending on application settings, workspace configurations, and user permissions. Thus, even when a manual describes a valid procedure, the agent should learn how to execute it robustly in the observed environment. To address this problem, we utilize user manuals not only for execution-time planning but also for policy training. As shown in Figure 2 , the training pipeline consists of three stages: (1) task generation, (2) episode generation, and (3) policy optimization. In the first stage, MAGE uses the manual to construct a set of executable task-plan pairs. This stage is performed once before training begins. Second, the current policy executes these task-plan pairs in the target GUI environment to collect episodes. Third, the collected episodes are evaluated and used to optimize the policy via GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . The second and third stages are repeated iteratively, so that each updated policy produces new episodes for subsequent optimization.

sections.heading: 3.3.1 Task Generation
sections.text: In this stage, MAGE generates a wide range of executable task instructions from the manual. Since policy optimization requires successful trajectories, training becomes ineffective when the initial policy rarely completes long-horizon GUI tasks. To address this, we generate plans together with tasks to guide execution and steer rollouts toward task-completing trajectories. For each manual section, MAGE uses both the textual content and images as inputs. A multimodal LLM interprets the functional descriptions and examples in the section, and generates a setup task ℐ setup \mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{setup}} , a setup plan 𝒫 setup \mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{setup}} , a main task ℐ main \mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{main}} , and a main plan 𝒫 main \mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{main}} . The setup task is an optional preliminary task that configures the initial GUI state required to execute the main task, while the main task is the final task that requires using the functionality described in the corresponding manual section. Each plan provides step-by-step procedural guidance for executing its corresponding task. By explicitly separating setup tasks, the framework can generate and execute diverse tasks without requiring manually prepared initial environments. The resulting setup and main tasks naturally involve common operations in the target program, such as entering values into spreadsheet cells or navigating application menus. Training on these tasks exposes the agent to frequently used program operations while covering diverse functionalities and usage procedures described in the manual. The prompt template for task generation is provided in Appendix F.1 .

sections.heading: 3.3.2 Episode Generation
sections.text: In this stage, trajectories are constructed by executing the generated task pairs in the GUI environment. The trajectory collection follows the interaction process described in Section 3.2 . When a setup task is included in a task pair, the agent first executes the setup task to configure the required GUI state, and proceeds to the main task only upon successful completion. If there is no setup task, the agent directly executes the main task from the initial state. Each task execution generates a trajectory τ = { ( o 1 , a 1 ) , ( o 2 , a 2 ) , … , ( o T , a T ) } \tau=\{(o_{1},a_{1}),(o_{2},a_{2}),\dots,(o_{T},a_{T})\} consisting of a sequence of observations and actions. To determine task success, we adopt the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm and employ a vision-language model (VLM) as an evaluator. The evaluator assigns a binary success reward R success ∈ { 0 , 1 } R^{\mathrm{success}}\in\{0,1\} to each trajectory, where R success = 1 R^{\mathrm{success}}=1 if the task is judged as successful and R success = 0 R^{\mathrm{success}}=0 otherwise. However, prior work ( Yang et al., 2025 ) has shown that evaluating full trajectories can be unreliable, as important details may be overlooked and hallucinations may lead to incorrect judgments. To mitigate this issue, we determine task success from the task instruction and the last five screenshots of the trajectory. This design aims to reduce susceptibility to hallucinations and evaluation cost. We provide a detailed analysis of the evaluator in Appendix D.3 . For policy optimization, we construct training episodes from the collected task executions. Setup and main tasks are handled as separate training instances rather than being merged into a single trajectory. Accordingly, each task execution produces a separate training episode, defined as a tuple ( ℐ , 𝒫 , τ , R success ) (\mathcal{I},\mathcal{P},\tau,R^{\mathrm{success}}) . Each task is executed multiple times to collect a diverse set of episodes, which are subsequently used for GRPO-based policy optimization.

sections.heading: 3.3.3 Policy Optimization with Manual-Derived Episodes
sections.text: In our adaptation setting, the amount of interaction data and available computation are limited compared to general foundation model training. Thus, we utilize GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) to optimize the CUA from collected episodes instead of using other reinforcement learning algorithms requiring a separate value model, such as PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) .

sections.heading: Round-based training
sections.text: GRPO requires multiple rollouts per task to estimate group-level statistics, and learning becomes more effective as the proportion of episodes with positive rewards increases. However, generating new rollouts at every training step incurs substantial computational cost. We define a round as a cycle of episode generation and GRPO-based training. To address this, we propose a round-based training strategy that builds on an offline learning setup by reusing existing data while incrementally incorporating rollouts generated by the latest policy. In each round, newly generated episodes are added to the existing dataset and used for subsequent training. By repeating this process, rollouts with higher success rates are progressively collected, enabling the dataset to expand and the policy to improve over time.

sections.heading: Episode sampling
sections.text: Instead of computing expectations over all episodes within a group, we adopt a sampling-based approximation. For each task, one episode is randomly sampled for training, while its advantage is computed using all available episodes in the group. In this process, setup tasks and main tasks are treated as distinct, independent task instances, and sampling is performed separately for each task. Due to the dependency between setup and main tasks, not all attempts result in valid episodes, and multiple trials for a given task may yield only a limited number of episodes. In particular, when all episodes for a given task have identical rewards or when only a single episode is available, the reward variance becomes zero, making advantage estimation ill-defined. To address this issue, we exclude episode groups with zero reward variance from policy optimization. This approach reduces computational overhead by reusing previously collected episodes rather than generating new rollouts at every training step.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Benchmarks and applications. We evaluate MAGE on the OSWorld benchmark ( Xie et al., 2024 ) for five applications: LibreOffice Calc, Impress, and Writer, GIMP, and VSCode. These applications require diverse multi-step GUI interactions including spreadsheet editing, slide modification, document editing, image editing, and code-related operations. Since OSWorld is a widely used CUA benchmark, tasks on these applications may already be in CUA training data. To examine whether MAGE can also adapt CUAs to applications with potentially limited coverage in their training, we construct 30 new evaluation tasks for Slack, a workplace communication platform.

sections.heading: Models
sections.text: We evaluate our framework with two CUA backbones: UI-TARS-1.5 (7B) ( Qin et al., 2025 ) and EvoCUA (8B) ( Xue et al., 2026 ) . For retrieval-augmented planning, we use Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) for manual retrieval and Qwen3.6 (27B) for plan generation. At the beginning of each task, the planner generates a task-specific plan conditioned on the task instruction, initial screenshot, and retrieved manual content. The generated plan remains fixed throughout execution. We use GPT-5.4 for manual-based task generation and trajectory evaluation during training.

We use the Round-based Training strategy described in Section 3.3.3 for policy optimization. Training is performed separately for each application to evaluate application-specific adaptation. Within each application, the training configuration differs between the UI-TARS-1.5 and EvoCUA backbones. Detailed backbone-specific settings, including the number of rounds and episodes generated per round, are provided in Appendix A.2 . Evaluation setup. To account for the inherent stochasticity of CUAs, we evaluate our main models over five independent runs on both OSWorld and Slack and report the mean and standard deviation. For OSWorld, we evaluate performance across five applications. Because the number of tasks differs across applications, the overall Success Rate (SR) is micro-averaged by dividing the total number of successful tasks by the total number of tasks across all applications. For the backbone models used in MAGE, the five runs include results from the official OSWorld dashboard (two for UI-TARS-1.5 and one for EvoCUA). To evaluate MAGE on Slack, we construct a separate test set consisting of 30 task pairs across 15 themes. sections.heading: 4.2 Main Results
sections.text: OSWorld. As shown in Table 1 , MAGE consistently improves performance across all five applications and both backbone models. To assess the statistical significance of the overall success rate improvement, we conduct a two-sided Welch’s t-test. The improvements are statistically significant for both UI-TARS-1.5 ( p = 4.13 × 10 − 4 p=4.13\times 10^{-4} ) and EvoCUA ( p = 3.63 × 10 − 4 p=3.63\times 10^{-4} ). Notable improvements are observed in Calc and VSCode, with gains of 19.57 %p for UI-TARS-1.5 on Calc and 10.43%p for EvoCUA on VSCode. Many tasks in Calc and VSCode can be performed using keyboard shortcuts or application-specific commands, potentially reducing the need for complex menu navigation. We hypothesize that MAGE benefits from retrieving these procedures from user manuals and incorporating them into its plans, helping agents execute tasks more effectively.

By leveraging user manuals for planning and policy optimization, MAGE may compensate for this lack of application-specific training experience, leading to larger performance gains on Slack. These results suggest its potential for adapting to new applications with limited prior training data.

sections.heading: 4.3 Analysis
sections.text: We provide additional analyses of MAGE using UI-TARS-1.5 as the backbone.

sections.heading: 4.3.1 Ablation Study
sections.text: We conduct an ablation study to evaluate the contributions of MAGE’s two key components: Retrieval-augmented Planning (RAP) during execution and Policy Optimization (PO) during training. The baseline and MAGE results are averaged over five independent runs, while the other variants are evaluated using a single run. With PO alone, the success rate is 0.42 percentage points (pp) higher than the baseline, whereas with RAP alone, it is 11.06 pp higher than the baseline. Combining RAP and PO provides an additional gain of 8.51 pp over RAP alone, resulting in a total improvement of 19.57 pp over the baseline. These results highlight the effectiveness of manual-guided planning and suggest that PO provides additional benefits when combined with RAP. sections.heading: 4.3.2 Qualitative Evaluation
sections.text: As shown in figure 3 , the vanilla CUA repeatedly executes a sequence of three distinct clicks 16 times, resulting in 48 unnecessary actions before reaching the maximum step budget of 50 and failing the task. In contrast, MAGE retrieves five relevant manual sections (Numbers as Text, Date and Time, Leading Zeroes, Manual Line Break, and Introduction) and generates a task execution plan based on the retrieved information. The resulting plan instructs the agent to use the Ctrl+1 shortcut to open the Format Cells dialog, enabling it to successfully complete the task in only five steps. Additionally, when the planner generates a plan without access to the retrieved manual sections, the agent still completes the task in seven steps by opening the Format Cells dialog through mouse clicks. These results show that providing a plan even without user manuals helps the agent avoid repetitive actions. Incorporating user manuals further enables the agent to leverage documented application-specific functionalities. This allows the agent to execute tasks more efficiently.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented MAGE, a framework that leverages user manuals for both task execution with manual-guided planning and training with manual-derived tasks. In the execution pipeline, MAGE retrieves task-relevant manual sections and uses a planner to generate a plan conditioned on the task instruction and the initial screen state. The generated plan is provided to CUAs, together with the task instruction and trajectory history, allowing them to incorporate external procedural knowledge during action generation. In the training pipeline, MAGE constructs manual-derived tasks from function-level manual sections, collects self-generated trajectories in the GUI environment, assigns rewards through an automatic evaluator, and performs GRPO-based policy optimization. This design integrates manual-based task construction, agent–environment interaction, reward assignment, and policy optimization without requiring human-authored expert demonstrations. Our experiments demonstrate that incorporating user manuals into planning and policy optimization improves task success across multiple applications. These results suggest that user manuals can be used not only as human-facing documentation, but also as scalable supervision for building more capable CUAs.

sections.heading: AI Use Statement
sections.text: In this work, we used generative AI tools to generate synthetic datasets; design and provide feedback on research methodology and experiments; implement methods; assist with translation; clean and reformat datasets; and support qualitative and thematic data analysis. We did not use generative AI tools to propose or refine hypotheses, develop theoretical models or conceptual frameworks, formulate mathematical claims, provide critical ingredients for proving mathematical claims, or interpret experimental results. All AI-assisted outputs were reviewed and validated by the authors. In particular, AI-generated tasks and plans were manually examined for usefulness, feasibility, requirement coverage, procedural correctness, executability, and scope safety. AI-assisted implementations were tested through controlled experiments and benchmark evaluations, and automatically generated trajectory assessments were cross-checked against the official rule-based evaluators. The authors independently analyzed and interpreted the experimental results. We take full responsibility for the final content of this work, including all text, claims, code, data, and other artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.text: This work aims to reduce the human demonstration effort required to adapt computer-using agents to target applications. Such agents may also cause unintended operations, data loss, or unauthorized actions. Our experiments evaluate task execution in designated test environments; the results do not establish safe deployment in unrestricted settings. Practical deployment should incorporate restricted permissions, user confirmation for sensitive actions, and appropriate logging. The safeguards discussed here are deployment recommendations rather than guarantees provided by our method.

sections.heading: Reproducibility Statement
sections.text: The main text and appendix describe the task-generation procedure, retrieval-augmented planning, policy optimization, and evaluation protocols. The appendix provides prompt templates, training configurations, action spaces, and additional analyses. To support reproducibility, we release the training and execution code, reproduction scripts, tasks, trajectories, and trained model checkpoints through the repository linked in the abstract. Because Slack requires account authentication, its execution trajectories may contain account-identifying information; we will therefore release them after removing such information.

sections.heading: User manuals
sections.text: We collect publicly available English user manuals for six applications: LibreOffice Calc, Impress, Writer, GIMP, VSCode, and Slack. For LibreOffice, we use Calc Guide 7.1 (May 2021), Impress Guide 7.6 (October 2023), and Writer Guide 7.3 (March 2022), respectively. For GIMP, we use the official GIMP 3.2 documentation. For VSCode and Slack, we collect documentation from their respective official websites, including the VSCode documentation and Slack Help Center.

sections.heading: Manual section segmentation
sections.text: We segment user manuals into section-level chunks based on their document structure. For LibreOffice, we divide the PDF manuals according to their tables of contents. For web-based documentation, including GIMP, VSCode, and Slack, we use HTML headings to define section boundaries.

sections.heading: Task generation
sections.text: Before task generation, we exclude manual sections covering introductory material, application overviews, version updates, file sharing, and operations requiring external resources or integration with other applications. For each retained section, we generate up to two tasks. We then sample a subset of the generated tasks to keep the number of training tasks manageable. For Slack, we further exclude features unavailable in a free workspace with administrator privileges.

sections.heading: Trajectory generation
sections.text: For each generated task, we collect trajectories over five independent runs. We report the number of generated trajectories, their average number of steps, and the training success rate (SR).

sections.heading: Agent inference setting
sections.text: Although the formulation conditions action generation on the full trajectory, our implementation uses only the five most recent screenshots as trajectory context. For fair comparison, we retain the OSWorld-provided configurations for UI-TARS-1.5 and EvoCUA during both training and inference. For both trajectory generation and evaluation, we use a maximum interaction budget of 50 steps.

sections.heading: A.2 Training Details
sections.text: Unless otherwise specified, training experiments are conducted on a server equipped with three NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

sections.heading: Common hyperparameters
sections.text: For both backbones, we set the step-efficiency reward weight to λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 , the clipping parameter to ϵ = 0.2 \epsilon=0.2 , and the KL penalty coefficient to β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 . These values remain fixed throughout training, without scheduling or adaptive adjustment. For retrieval-augmented planning, we retrieve the top- K K manual sections with K = 5 K=5 , unless otherwise specified.

sections.heading: UI-TARS-1.5
sections.text: We fine-tune UI-TARS-1.5-7B using LoRA ( Hu et al., 2021 ) with rank 16 and scaling parameter α = 32 \alpha=32 , applied to the query, value, and output projection layers. We use the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 5 1\times 10^{-5} . Training is conducted over two rounds. In the first round, we generate three rollouts per task and train for two epochs. In the second round, we generate two rollouts per task and again train for two epochs.

sections.heading: EvoCUA
sections.text: We fine-tune EvoCUA-8B using LoRA with rank 8 and scaling parameter α = 16 \alpha=16 , applied to the query, value, and output projection layers. We use the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 6 1\times 10^{-6} . We observed that EvoCUA tends to overfit more quickly than UI-TARS-1.5 under our training setup, and therefore conduct only a single training round for EvoCUA. In this round, we generate five rollouts per task and train for two epochs.

sections.heading: A.3 Computational Cost for VSCode
sections.text: Unlike the other applications, the VSCode experiments were conducted on six NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs due to hardware availability. Adapting MAGE to VSCode incurred an API cost of $91.25, with 73.43 hours required for episode generation and 34.65 hours for policy optimization, resulting in a total wall-clock time of 108.08 hours. Because the VSCode experiments were conducted under a different GPU configuration from the H100-based experiments, we report these computational costs separately rather than directly comparing their wall-clock time with those of the other applications.

sections.heading: F.1 Manual-Derived Task Generation Prompt
sections.text: We use the following prompt to generate manual-derived task samples from each manual section. The same prompt template is used across applications, while the input program name, manual section text, and section images are replaced for each section. Placeholders enclosed in braces denote instance-specific inputs. Manual-Derived Task Generation Prompt ⬇ You are an expert at generating GUI - based practice tasks for AI agents . You will be given : 1. Program name 2. One section of manual text , which may span multiple pages 3. One or more images from the manual section Your task is to generate executable GUI practice tasks based strictly on the given manual section . Each task must be output as an instruction pair with : - setup instruction , if necessary - main instruction Each instruction must contain : - task : a short sentence describing the goal - steps : a list of concrete GUI actions Rules : 1. Generate up to two task samples , or none if the section is irrelevant . 2. The task must produce a visible result on the screen . Do not generate tasks such as : - opening menus only - checking whether a feature exists - saving a file - exploring the UI The result must be visually observable , such as formatted text , a created chart , a changed slide object , or hidden columns . 3. The starting screen is always a freshly opened blank / default screen . No files , tables , documents , slides , conversations , or other pre - existing content are assumed . 4. The GUI agent must not be asked to make subjective or free choices . Do not generate steps such as : - choose any color - select a preferred style - pick an option you like - apply a random format All actions must be deterministic and explicitly specified . 5. Output format : [ { " setup_task ": "...", " setup_steps ": [...], " main_task ": "...", " main_steps ": [...], " id ": 0 } ] 6. Setup instruction : - Setup is only for creating or preparing data or objects required by the main task . - If the main task needs any pre - existing value , text , table , slide object , or conversation content , it must be created in setup_steps . - Main steps must never include data creation actions such as typing initial values , creating tables , or preparing sample objects . - If the main task can be done from a blank screen without preparation , leave setup_task as an empty string and setup_steps as an empty list . 7. Main instruction : - Main steps must only apply the manual feature to the prepared data or objects . - Main steps must not include : - entering initial numbers or text - creating tables - preparing sample data - creating initial objects - Main task must be a concrete exercise reconstructed from the manual section . 8. If sample data or objects are required in setup : - Do not rely only on images . - Describe exactly how to create the required data or objects in text steps . 9. Steps must : - be atomic GUI actions , such as click , type , select , drag , or press keys - be ordered - not include explanations - not mention the manual or images 10. Do not invent features not mentioned in the given manual section . 11. Section - based multimodal input handling : - The text is section - level , not single - page . - Multiple images may be provided for the same section . - Use all provided images as supporting context when relevant . - If text and images conflict , prioritize the manual text . - Do not assume hidden UI details not visible in the text or images . 12. Output must be only valid JSON . - No markdown - No explanation - No extra text Input : Program name : { program_name } Manual section text : { manual_section_text } Manual section images : { manual_section_images }

sections.heading: F.2 Manual-Guided Plan Generation Prompt
sections.text: This prompt is used to generate a task-specific plan during Manual-Guided Planning. It takes the task instruction, the initial screenshot, and retrieved manual sections as input, and outputs a concise step-by-step plan that guides the CUA during action generation. Manual-Guided Plan Generation Prompt ⬇ You are a planner for a GUI agent operating on real screenshots . You will be given : 1) A task instruction 2) The initial screenshot of the environment 3) Potentially relevant manual snippets retrieved for this task Your goal is to generate a concise , step - by - step plan that the agent can follow to complete the task . Requirements : - Focus only on actions that are directly useful for completing the task . - Each step must correspond to a realistic GUI interaction , such as click , type , scroll , or select . - Ground each step in visible UI elements from the initial screenshot , such as button labels , menus , input fields , icons , or relative positions . - Prefer explicit interaction targets , such as clicking the Insert menu at the top toolbar , instead of vague descriptions . - If multiple paths are possible , choose the most straightforward and reliable one . - Avoid assumptions about hidden UI or unavailable elements . - If the UI element is not clearly visible , describe how to locate it , such as via menu navigation or scrolling . - Do not include unnecessary explanations , reasoning , or background knowledge . - Do not repeat the task instruction . Robustness : - If an action might fail , suggest a simple alternative interaction , such as using a button instead of typing . - Ensure the plan is executable even with minor UI variations . Output format : - Output only one section titled " Relevant plan ". - Use short , ordered , numbered steps . - Each step should describe exactly one action . Input : Task instruction : { task_instruction } Initial screenshot : { initial_screenshot } Retrieved manual sections : { retrieved_manual_sections }

sections.heading: F.3 Trajectory Evaluation Prompt
sections.text: The evaluator outputs both a binary success label and a continuous progress score. The progress score is used only for consistency checking and is not used as a training reward. For policy optimization, we assign rewards based on the binary success label. Trajectory Evaluation Prompt ⬇ You are an evaluation agent . You will be provided with : 1. The Task objective 2. The last 5 images of the task trajectory . Your tasks consist of two parts : PART 1: Task Success Evaluation - Determine whether the Task objective has been successfully completed . - Evaluate this by referring to : - the visual evidence in the last 5 step images - Do not rely only on the final image ; consider transitions and changes across all five images . - Carefully analyze visual information and logical progression step - by - step . PART 2: Task Progress Evaluation - Evaluate how much the Task has progressed toward completion . - Use : - the visual evidence across the last 5 step images - Do NOT rely only on the final image . - Compare observed behavior strictly against the Task requirements . - The score should reflect how much of the Task has been completed so far , not just whether it succeeded or failed . Scoring Guidelines : - Assign a score between 0.0 and 1.0 in increments of 0.01. - 0.00 = no meaningful progress toward the Task goal - 1.00 = Task fully completed - Intermediate values should represent proportional progress . - Consider : - how many required steps have been completed - how correct the completed steps are - whether errors block further progress Output Rules : - Output MUST be valid JSON . - Do NOT include any text outside the JSON object . - Always output the score as a JSON number , not a string . Output format : { " result_thought ": " Explain , step - by - step , how you analyzed the last 5 images and why you concluded that the Task succeeded or failed .", " result ": " SUCCESS " or " FAIL ", " score_thought ": " Explain , step - by - step , how you analyzed the last 5 images and why you assigned this progress score .", " score ": 0.00 }

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.23012v1 [cs.AI] 16 Oct 2026 Adaptation of Computer Use Agents to New Software with User Manuals Chulhoon Yoon Affiliation: Korea University Kyungri Park Affiliation: Hanyang University Jinyeong Yun Affiliation: Korea University Daeyun Jeong Affiliation: Hanyang University Sukmin Yun Affiliation: Hanyang University Woohwan Jung Affiliation: Korea University Abstract Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have significantly improved the ability to operate real-world software through graphical user interfaces (GUIs) using visual observations and natural language instructions. However, maintaining strong performance on unseen applications remains challenging, as practical tasks often require long-horizon procedural knowledge and application-specific operation patterns. In addition, constructing executable tasks and collecting corresponding trajectories for training still heavily rely on human-annotated data, incurring substantial cost. In this paper, we propose MAGE (Manual-augmented computer use AG ent E xecution and learning), a framework that leverages user manuals as a scalable source of procedural knowledge to improve both inference and training. During execution, MAGE retrieves task-relevant manual content and uses a planner to generate explicit procedural guidance for CUAs. To further account for the discrepancies between manuals and actual GUI environments, such as version differences or user settings, MAGE also adapts the agent policy through environment interaction. During training, MAGE converts manuals into executable task-plan pairs and uses the plans to guide environment rollouts toward task-relevant states; the resulting trajectories are then used to optimize the policy without human-authored demonstrations. This unified design enables effective utilization of manuals for both task execution and training, reducing reliance on human-authored training data. Experimental results across six applications demonstrate improvements in task success rates over strong baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of manual-guided planning and policy adaptation in new software environments. We provide the code and reproduction scripts at https://github.com/ku-autoai/MAGE.git . 1 Introduction Recent advances in multimodal vision-language models (VLMs) ( Yin et al., 2024 ) have enabled Computer Use Agents (CUAs) ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) to operate software from visual observations and natural language instructions. Unlike conventional automation methods that rely on APIs or HTML structures, these agents interact directly with graphical user interfaces (GUIs) in a human-like manner. This enables CUAs to perform various tasks across diverse software environments. However, existing CUAs require additional training to maintain high performance on unfamiliar applications since each application has its own interface and functionalities. Existing adaptation ( Qin et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) typically relies on costly human annotations to define diverse executable tasks and collect corresponding action trajectories. Although reinforcement learning ( Sutton et al., 1998 ; Silver and Sutton, 2025 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) can reduce the need for human demonstrations, GUI tasks are inherently long-horizon: agents should sequentially uncover available options through clicks, menus, and dialogs rather than observing all relevant information at once. This makes it difficult to obtain sufficient successful trajectories, limiting the training signals required to improve the agent policy. To address these limitations, we leverage user manuals as a source of procedural supervision. Manuals describe application functionalities and the procedures required to execute them, including functions hidden behind menus, dialogs, and toolbars. By exposing access routes to such functions, manuals can reduce unguided exploration in long-horizon GUI tasks. Prior approaches have also leveraged external knowledge, such as web tutorials and past interaction experiences, to guide GUI agents ( Xu et al., 2025a ; Agashe et al., 2025 ) . However, providing external knowledge only during execution does not directly address the challenge of collecting successful trajectories for policy adaptation. Moreover, manuals may be abstract or differ from actual GUI environments due to software versions, user settings, or access permissions. Thus, agents must ground procedural guidance through environment interaction and learn which actions succeed in the current GUI state. Based on this observation, we propose MAGE (Manual-augmented computer use AG ent E xecution and learning), a unified framework that leverages user manuals to improve both execution-time planning and training-time policy optimization. During execution, MAGE retrieves task-relevant manual content and uses a planner to generate task-specific procedural plans that guide CUAs. During training, it automatically generates diverse executable tasks and corresponding plans from user manuals. Rather than treating generated plans as expert demonstrations, MAGE evaluates the collected trajectories and optimizes the agent policy using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). This joint use of manuals for planning and policy learning enables application-specific adaptation without human-authored demonstrations or step-level action annotations. Our main contributions are summarized as follows. • We propose MAGE, a unified framework that uses user manuals as procedural supervision for both execution-time planning and training-time policy learning, combining a planner with CUAs. • We introduce retrieval-augmented planning, which retrieves task-relevant manual content and generates procedural plans to guide long-horizon GUI execution. • We develop a manual-derived training method that constructs task-plan pairs and optimizes the policy from the resulting trajectories without human-authored demonstrations or step-level annotations. • We evaluate MAGE across six applications and demonstrate improvements in task success rates over the corresponding baselines, examining the contributions of manual-guided planning and policy optimization. 2 Related Work Computer use agents (CUAs) To mitigate reliance on specific interfaces or predefined structural representations in computer environments, VLM-based agents that understand GUIs purely from visual signals have been proposed, with representative examples including OpenCUA ( Wang et al., 2025 ) and UI-TARS ( Qin et al., 2025 ) . Training these foundation models requires large and diverse datasets. For instance, OpenCUA ( Wang et al., 2025 ) integrates datasets from prior works such as ShowUI ( Lin et al., 2024 ) and UGround ( Qian et al., 2025 ) , along with general supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data from the Kimi Team ( Team et al., 2025 ) , and further incorporates demonstration data collected from Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS environments. Similarly, UI-TARS ( Qin et al., 2025 ) constructs additional training data by allowing human annotators to refine and correct trajectories generated by the model. While such data-centric training strategies significantly improve model performance, adapting these models to new software environments requires additional data collection and annotation tailored to each target domain. This process incurs substantial cost, thereby limiting the scalability and practical applicability of CUAs. Reducing human supervision for CUA adaptation Prior work has explored reducing human supervision for CUA adaptation by augmenting or reusing existing datasets for training, or by leveraging external knowledge to guide task execution. BTL-UI ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) augments existing datasets with ROI annotations, while ZeroGUI ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and DART ( Li et al., 2025 ) leverage benchmark-derived tasks for reinforcement learning. Meanwhile, RAG-GUI ( Xu et al., 2025a ) trains a VLM to generate guidelines from web tutorials, guiding a frozen CUA at inference time, and Agent S ( Agashe et al., 2025 ) uses external knowledge for hierarchical planning. However, data-driven approaches still rely on task-specific data, while knowledge-based approaches primarily assist execution at inference time without adapting the CUA’s policy. In contrast, MAGE leverages user manuals for both planning and policy optimization, improving task execution without repeatedly generating plans throughout an episode. 3 Method MAGE is a manual-augmented adaptation framework for CUAs. Given a target program and its user manual, MAGE uses the manual as procedural supervision in two complementary ways: it retrieves task-relevant instructions to guide long-horizon execution, and it generates executable task-plan pairs to support policy training. These two components address the main bottlenecks in GUI adaptation: reliable task execution and scalable collection of successful trajectories. 3.1 Problem Definition Given a natural language task instruction ℐ \mathcal{I} , our goal is to complete the task ℐ \mathcal{I} by performing a sequence of actions. At each time step t t , the agent observes a screenshot o t o_{t} , generates an action a t a_{t} , and receives the next observation o t + 1 o_{t+1} . This process forms a trajectory τ = { ( o 1 , a 1 ) , ( o 2 , a 2 ) , … , ( o T , a T ) } \tau=\{(o_{1},a_{1}),(o_{2},a_{2}),\dots,(o_{T},a_{T})\} where T T is the length of the trajectory. The action space includes common mouse and keyboard actions such as click, right click, double click, scroll, drag, and typing. Please refer to Appendix E for the detailed descriptions of each action and its arguments. 3.2 Task Execution with Retrieval-Augmented Planning Figure 1: Task execution with user manuals. MAGE retrieves relevant manual sections, then generates a retrieval-augmented plan, and finally performs GUI task execution conditioned on the plan. CUAs execute a task by repeatedly selecting the most appropriate action a t a_{t} based on the current observation o t o_{t} and the past trajectory τ < t = { ( o j , a j ) | 1 ≤ j < t } \tau_{<t}=\{(o_{j},a_{j})|1\leq j<t\} . However, in many GUI environments, the information required for the task completion is not fully visible in the current screenshot. Important functions are often hidden behind menus, dialogs, toolbars, or keyboard shortcuts, degrading the performance of agents for long-horizon tasks. To address the problem, we propose retrieval-augmented planning which uses procedural guidance from user manuals during task execution. As shown in Figure 1 , our task execution consists of two stages. In the first stage, MAGE performs retrieval-augmented planning, following the retrieval-augmented generation framework ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) . It first retrieves relevant manual sections to provide detailed procedural information to the planner and generates an execution plan consisting of a sequence of actions with specific information such as button names and keyboard shortcuts. In the next stage, MAGE executes the task similarly to conventional CUAs but with the execution plan. Retrieval-augmented planning MAGE retrieves manual sections relevant to ℐ \mathcal{I} and generates a task-specific plan. Let ℳ = { m 1 , … , m | M | } \mathcal{M}=\{m_{1},\ldots,m_{|M|}\} denote the set of manual sections. We encode each manual section m i m_{i} using an embedding model as 𝐡 i = E ⁡ ( m i ) \mathbf{h}_{i}=E(m_{i}) . The embedding vectors are indexed in a vector database before executing the CUA. To retrieve the relevant section, MAGE encodes the task instruction as 𝐪 = E ⁡ ( ℐ ) \mathbf{q}=E(\mathcal{I}) and finds the top- K K sections ℳ ℐ \mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{I}} with the highest cosine similarity cos ⁡ ( 𝐪 , 𝐡 i ) \cos(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{h}_{i}) . The planner then takes the task instruction ℐ \mathcal{I} , the relevant sections ℳ ℐ \mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{I}} , and the initial observation o 1 o_{1} as inputs, and generates a plan 𝒫 \mathcal{P} that includes step-by-step procedures with specific actions. We use a multimodal LLM as the planner and provide its prompt in Appendix F.2 . Task execution with the generated plan Given the generated plan, MAGE executes the task by conditioning the CUA on the task instruction ℐ \mathcal{I} , the plan 𝒫 \mathcal{P} , the current observation o t o_{t} , and the past trajectory τ < t \tau_{<t} . At each time t t , the agent selects the next action as a t ∼ π θ ( ⋅ | o t , τ < t , 𝒫 , ℐ ) . a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|o_{t},\tau_{<t},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{I}). (1) The plan remains fixed throughout the episode, while the CUA selects actions based on the current observation and interaction history. 3.3 Training CUAs with Manual-Derived Tasks Figure 2: Training CUAs with a user manual. MAGE uses manual-derived task-plan pairs to collect episodes for policy optimization. Retrieval-augmented planning provides procedural guidance, but manuals do not fully specify the actual GUI state of a target environment. In addition, interface elements can be hidden, customized, or restricted depending on application settings, workspace configurations, and user permissions. Thus, even when a manual describes a valid procedure, the agent should learn how to execute it robustly in the observed environment. To address this problem, we utilize user manuals not only for execution-time planning but also for policy training. As shown in Figure 2 , the training pipeline consists of three stages: (1) task generation, (2) episode generation, and (3) policy optimization. In the first stage, MAGE uses the manual to construct a set of executable task-plan pairs. This stage is performed once before training begins. Second, the current policy executes these task-plan pairs in the target GUI environment to collect episodes. Third, the collected episodes are evaluated and used to optimize the policy via GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . The second and third stages are repeated iteratively, so that each updated policy produces new episodes for subsequent optimization. 3.3.1 Task Generation In this stage, MAGE generates a wide range of executable task instructions from the manual. Since policy optimization requires successful trajectories, training becomes ineffective when the initial policy rarely completes long-horizon GUI tasks. To address this, we generate plans together with tasks to guide execution and steer rollouts toward task-completing trajectories. For each manual section, MAGE uses both the textual content and images as inputs. A multimodal LLM interprets the functional descriptions and examples in the section, and generates a setup task ℐ setup \mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{setup}} , a setup plan 𝒫 setup \mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{setup}} , a main task ℐ main \mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{main}} , and a main plan 𝒫 main \mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{main}} . The setup task is an optional preliminary task that configures the initial GUI state required to execute the main task, while the main task is the final task that requires using the functionality described in the corresponding manual section. Each plan provides step-by-step procedural guidance for executing its corresponding task. By explicitly separating setup tasks, the framework can generate and execute diverse tasks without requiring manually prepared initial environments. The resulting setup and main tasks naturally involve common operations in the target program, such as entering values into spreadsheet cells or navigating application menus. Training on these tasks exposes the agent to frequently used program operations while covering diverse functionalities and usage procedures described in the manual. The prompt template for task generation is provided in Appendix F.1 . 3.3.2 Episode Generation In this stage, trajectories are constructed by executing the generated task pairs in the GUI environment. The trajectory collection follows the interaction process described in Section 3.2 . When a setup task is included in a task pair, the agent first executes the setup task to configure the required GUI state, and proceeds to the main task only upon successful completion. If there is no setup task, the agent directly executes the main task from the initial state. Each task execution generates a trajectory τ = { ( o 1 , a 1 ) , ( o 2 , a 2 ) , … , ( o T , a T ) } \tau=\{(o_{1},a_{1}),(o_{2},a_{2}),\dots,(o_{T},a_{T})\} consisting of a sequence of observations and actions. To determine task success, we adopt the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm and employ a vision-language model (VLM) as an evaluator. The evaluator assigns a binary success reward R success ∈ { 0 , 1 } R^{\mathrm{success}}\in\{0,1\} to each trajectory, where R success = 1 R^{\mathrm{success}}=1 if the task is judged as successful and R success = 0 R^{\mathrm{success}}=0 otherwise. However, prior work ( Yang et al., 2025 ) has shown that evaluating full trajectories can be unreliable, as important details may be overlooked and hallucinations may lead to incorrect judgments. To mitigate this issue, we determine task success from the task instruction and the last five screenshots of the trajectory. This design aims to reduce susceptibility to hallucinations and evaluation cost. We provide a detailed analysis of the evaluator in Appendix D.3 . For policy optimization, we construct training episodes from the collected task executions. Setup and main tasks are handled as separate training instances rather than being merged into a single trajectory. Accordingly, each task execution produces a separate training episode, defined as a tuple ( ℐ , 𝒫 , τ , R success ) (\mathcal{I},\mathcal{P},\tau,R^{\mathrm{success}}) . Each task is executed multiple times to collect a diverse set of episodes, which are subsequently used for GRPO-based policy optimization. 3.3.3 Policy Optimization with Manual-Derived Episodes In our adaptation setting, the amount of interaction data and available computation are limited compared to general foundation model training. Thus, we utilize GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) to optimize the CUA from collected episodes instead of using other reinforcement learning algorithms requiring a separate value model, such as PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) . Round-based training GRPO requires multiple rollouts per task to estimate group-level statistics, and learning becomes more effective as the proportion of episodes with positive rewards increases. However, generating new rollouts at every training step incurs substantial computational cost. We define a round as a cycle of episode generation and GRPO-based training. To address this, we propose a round-based training strategy that builds on an offline learning setup by reusing existing data while incrementally incorporating rollouts generated by the latest policy. In each round, newly generated episodes are added to the existing dataset and used for subsequent training. By repeating this process, rollouts with higher success rates are progressively collected, enabling the dataset to expand and the policy to improve over time. Episode sampling Instead of computing expectations over all episodes within a group, we adopt a sampling-based approximation. For each task, one episode is randomly sampled for training, while its advantage is computed using all available episodes in the group. In this process, setup tasks and main tasks are treated as distinct, independent task instances, and sampling is performed separately for each task. Due to the dependency between setup and main tasks, not all attempts result in valid episodes, and multiple trials for a given task may yield only a limited number of episodes. In particular, when all episodes for a given task have identical rewards or when only a single episode is available, the reward variance becomes zero, making advantage estimation ill-defined. To address this issue, we exclude episode groups with zero reward variance from policy optimization. This approach reduces computational overhead by reusing previously collected episodes rather than generating new rollouts at every training step. Reward design We define the reward function based on both task success and execution efficiency. Let τ i \tau_{i} denote the i i -th trajectory with length T i T_{i} , and R i R_{i} denote the corresponding trajectory-level reward. We use the success reward R i success R_{i}^{\mathrm{success}} defined in Section 3.3.2 . At the beginning of each training epoch, we reset the old policy to the current policy. We evaluate MAGE on the OSWorld benchmark ( Xie et al., 2024 ) for five applications: LibreOffice Calc, Impress, and Writer, GIMP, and VSCode. These applications require diverse multi-step GUI interactions including spreadsheet editing, slide modification, document editing, image editing, and code-related operations. Since OSWorld is a widely used CUA benchmark, tasks on these applications may already be in CUA training data. To examine whether MAGE can also adapt CUAs to applications with potentially limited coverage in their training, we construct 30 new evaluation tasks for Slack, a workplace communication platform. Models We evaluate our framework with two CUA backbones: UI-TARS-1.5 (7B) ( Qin et al., 2025 ) and EvoCUA (8B) ( Xue et al., 2026 ) . For retrieval-augmented planning, we use Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) for manual retrieval and Qwen3.6 (27B) for plan generation. At the beginning of each task, the planner generates a task-specific plan conditioned on the task instruction, initial screenshot, and retrieved manual content. The generated plan remains fixed throughout execution. We use GPT-5.4 for manual-based task generation and trajectory evaluation during training. Training and planning setup For LibreOffice applications, we use the official LibreOffice user manuals 1 1 1 https://documentation.libreoffice.org/en/english-documentation/ for both retrieval-augmented planning and manual-derived task construction. For GIMP 2 2 2 https://docs.gimp.org/3.2/en/ and VSCode 3 3 3 https://code.visualstudio.com/docs , we use their official documentation, and for Slack, we use the Slack Help Center 4 4 4 https://slack.com/help . We use the Round-based Training strategy described in Section 3.3.3 for policy optimization. Training is performed separately for each application to evaluate application-specific adaptation. Within each application, the training configuration differs between the UI-TARS-1.5 and EvoCUA backbones. Detailed backbone-specific settings, including the number of rounds and episodes generated per round, are provided in Appendix A.2 . Evaluation setup. To account for the inherent stochasticity of CUAs, we evaluate our main models over five independent runs on both OSWorld and Slack and report the mean and standard deviation. For OSWorld, we evaluate performance across five applications. Because the number of tasks differs across applications, the overall Success Rate (SR) is micro-averaged by dividing the total number of successful tasks by the total number of tasks across all applications. For the backbone models used in MAGE, the five runs include results from the official OSWorld dashboard (two for UI-TARS-1.5 and one for EvoCUA). To evaluate MAGE on Slack, we construct a separate test set consisting of 30 task pairs across 15 themes. For Slack evaluation, we use Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview to determine task success from the task instruction and the last five screenshots of each trajectory. When a setup task is present, the agent must complete it before attempting the main task. We report the Success Rate (SR) across all 30 task pairs based on successful completion of the main task. Further details on the Slack evaluation are provided in Appendix B . Table 1: Task success rates (%) on OSWorld applications under a 50-step budget. In the execution pipeline, MAGE retrieves task-relevant manual sections and uses a planner to generate a plan conditioned on the task instruction and the initial screen state. The generated plan is provided to CUAs, together with the task instruction and trajectory history, allowing them to incorporate external procedural knowledge during action generation. In the training pipeline, MAGE constructs manual-derived tasks from function-level manual sections, collects self-generated trajectories in the GUI environment, assigns rewards through an automatic evaluator, and performs GRPO-based policy optimization. This design integrates manual-based task construction, agent–environment interaction, reward assignment, and policy optimization without requiring human-authored expert demonstrations. Our experiments demonstrate that incorporating user manuals into planning and policy optimization improves task success across multiple applications. These results suggest that user manuals can be used not only as human-facing documentation, but also as scalable supervision for building more capable CUAs. Appendix F Prompts F.1 Manual-Derived Task Generation Prompt We use the following prompt to generate manual-derived task samples from each manual section. The same prompt template is used across applications, while the input program name, manual section text, and section images are replaced for each section. Placeholders enclosed in braces denote instance-specific inputs. Manual-Derived Task Generation Prompt ⬇ You are an expert at generating GUI - based practice tasks for AI agents . You will be given : 1. Program name 2. One section of manual text , which may span multiple pages 3. One or more images from the manual section Your task is to generate executable GUI practice tasks based strictly on the given manual section . Each task must be output as an instruction pair with : - setup instruction , if necessary - main instruction Each instruction must contain : - task : a short sentence describing the goal - steps : a list of concrete GUI actions Rules : 1. Generate up to two task samples , or none if the section is irrelevant . 2. The task must produce a visible result on the screen . Do not generate tasks such as : - opening menus only - checking whether a feature exists - saving a file - exploring the UI The result must be visually observable , such as formatted text , a created chart , a changed slide object , or hidden columns . 3. The starting screen is always a freshly opened blank / default screen . No files , tables , documents , slides , conversations , or other pre - existing content are assumed . 4. The GUI agent must not be asked to make subjective or free choices . Do not generate steps such as : - choose any color - select a preferred style - pick an option you like - apply a random format All actions must be deterministic and explicitly specified . 5. Output format : [ { " setup_task ": "...", " setup_steps ": [...], " main_task ": "...", " main_steps ": [...], " id ": 0 } ] 6. Setup instruction : - Setup is only for creating or preparing data or objects required by the main task . - If the main task needs any pre - existing value , text , table , slide object , or conversation content , it must be created in setup_steps . - Main steps must never include data creation actions such as typing initial values , creating tables , or preparing sample objects . - If the main task can be done from a blank screen without preparation , leave setup_task as an empty string and setup_steps as an empty list . 7. Main instruction : - Main steps must only apply the manual feature to the prepared data or objects . - Main steps must not include : - entering initial numbers or text - creating tables - preparing sample data - creating initial objects - Main task must be a concrete exercise reconstructed from the manual section . 8. If sample data or objects are required in setup : - Do not rely only on images . - Describe exactly how to create the required data or objects in text steps . 9. Steps must : - be atomic GUI actions , such as click , type , select , drag , or press keys - be ordered - not include explanations - not mention the manual or images 10. Do not invent features not mentioned in the given manual section . 11. Section - based multimodal input handling : - The text is section - level , not single - page . - Multiple images may be provided for the same section . - Use all provided images as supporting context when relevant . - If text and images conflict , prioritize the manual text . - Do not assume hidden UI details not visible in the text or images . 12. Output must be only valid JSON . - No markdown - No explanation - No extra text Input : Program name : { program_name } Manual section text : { manual_section_text } Manual section images : { manual_section_images } F.2 Manual-Guided Plan Generation Prompt This prompt is used to generate a task-specific plan during Manual-Guided Planning. It takes the task instruction, the initial screenshot, and retrieved manual sections as input, and outputs a concise step-by-step plan that guides the CUA during action generation. Manual-Guided Plan Generation Prompt ⬇ You are a planner for a GUI agent operating on real screenshots . You will be given : 1) A task instruction 2) The initial screenshot of the environment 3) Potentially relevant manual snippets retrieved for this task Your goal is to generate a concise , step - by - step plan that the agent can follow to complete the task . Requirements : - Focus only on actions that are directly useful for completing the task . - Each step must correspond to a realistic GUI interaction , such as click , type , scroll , or select . - Ground each step in visible UI elements from the initial screenshot , such as button labels , menus , input fields , icons , or relative positions . - Prefer explicit interaction targets , such as clicking the Insert menu at the top toolbar , instead of vague descriptions . - If multiple paths are possible , choose the most straightforward and reliable one . - Avoid assumptions about hidden UI or unavailable elements . - If the UI element is not clearly visible , describe how to locate it , such as via menu navigation or scrolling . - Do not include unnecessary explanations , reasoning , or background knowledge . - Do not repeat the task instruction . Robustness : - If an action might fail , suggest a simple alternative interaction , such as using a button instead of typing . - Ensure the plan is executable even with minor UI variations . Output format : - Output only one section titled " Relevant plan ". - Use short , ordered , numbered steps . - Each step should describe exactly one action . Input : Task instruction : { task_instruction } Initial screenshot : { initial_screenshot } Retrieved manual sections : { retrieved_manual_sections } F.3 Trajectory Evaluation Prompt The evaluator outputs both a binary success label and a continuous progress score. The progress score is used only for consistency checking and is not used as a training reward. For policy optimization, we assign rewards based on the binary success label. Trajectory Evaluation Prompt ⬇ You are an evaluation agent . You will be provided with : 1. The Task objective 2. The last 5 images of the task trajectory . Your tasks consist of two parts : PART 1: Task Success Evaluation - Determine whether the Task objective has been successfully completed . - Evaluate this by referring to : - the visual evidence in the last 5 step images - Do not rely only on the final image ; consider transitions and changes across all five images . - Carefully analyze visual information and logical progression step - by - step . PART 2: Task Progress Evaluation - Evaluate how much the Task has progressed toward completion . - Use : - the visual evidence across the last 5 step images - Do NOT rely only on the final image . - Compare observed behavior strictly against the Task requirements . - The score should reflect how much of the Task has been completed so far , not just whether it succeeded or failed . Scoring Guidelines : - Assign a score between 0.0 and 1.0 in increments of 0.01. - 0.00 = no meaningful progress toward the Task goal - 1.00 = Task fully completed - Intermediate values should represent proportional progress . - Consider : - how many required steps have been completed - how correct the completed steps are - whether errors block further progress Output Rules : - Output MUST be valid JSON . - Do NOT include any text outside the JSON object . - Always output the score as a JSON number , not a string . Output format : { " result_thought ": " Explain , step - by - step , how you analyzed the last 5 images and why you concluded that the Task succeeded or failed .", " result ": " SUCCESS " or " FAIL ", " score_thought ": " Explain , step - by - step , how you analyzed the last 5 images and why you assigned this progress score .", " score ": 0.00 }
